Also, you can barely see it, but on the left side of the wall, there is a U of I pennant left by a previous student.  It always makes me smile when I see it.


I apologize for the vertical photo, but I think it captures the room a little better than horizontal.  Anyways, this is my bathroom. If you remember, this would be the second door on the left in that main hallway.  Its been really nice to have my own bathroom, because I don't have to worry about interrupting anyone's schedule. 

This photo was taken in that doorway that was at the end of the main hall.  My room is the one on the right.  Begoña's room is the one on the left.  There is another door on the left that is not pictured which leads to the bathroom. I really love the picture on the wall.  It shows her two family crests.  That of her mother and that of her father.


Here is that bathroom I was just talking about

If you poked your head in that door on the right, you would see this little room right before Begoña's bedroom. 


Finally, you see my bedroom!! I get some nice big windows with a view of the street.  Right now it is kind of noisy because of the construction, but it is nice to poke my head out and look down the beautiful street.. Again, a couple stringed instruments are hiding in the corner.


Then I took this picture from the other side of the bed. There is no shortage of space as I get these three large armoires to put my stuff in. 


So here you have seen my living arrangements. I couldn't tell you if this is the normal for Spain, because I haven't been in anyone else's apartments, but it has been treating me very well during the last week.  All is well over here in España, thanks for reading!

title: Bilbao Weekend
content:
So this week I didn´t have any big trips out of the country, but it still sure was a memorable one



I´m going to start this blog talking about food, because everyone loves food!

This is a pintxo that I had of "tortilla de patata" which is like an omlette with potatoes in the middle


Next up is some ribs with thinly sliced potatoes.


I'm not sure if I have mentioned this yet, but the people here love their purees here.  We probably have one or two a week.



So this next one is mussels with rice, which is interesting because I have a shellfish allergy. However, I ate it anyways because I'm young and stupid.  When I came home one day, Begoña showed me the dish very proudly telling me it was one of her favorites and that she couldn't wait to see what I thought.  I really did want to try it, and so I decided to google "can I eat mussels with a shellfish allergy".  Great search terms right?? Well, it turns out that there are two categories of shellfish: crustacea and mollusks.  Custacea is crabs, shrimp, lobster and mollusks is squid, octopus, mussels, clams, scallops. I figured that because I was fine when I tried octopus and squid, I should be okay with mussels.  So I ate it, and here I am typing this blog!


One random thing real quick, there are always pigeons in our school.  They tend to leave the doors wide open.  Its not really a big deal because the weather is always so nice, but the pigeons get in to scavange for food. Its kinda startling when they fly over your head in the hallways.  I took this picture from the schools little cafe.  They were inside eating food, but I didn't notice them until they flew right past my face.


Hair Cut


On Monday, I finally decided that I had time to go get my haircut.  My friend Matt told me about this awesome Brazilian guy by his house that cut hair for 10
Euro.  So Matt showed me were it was on a map and I headed over there.  When I got there I saw a barber shop and so I walked right in.  As soon as I sat down inside I realized I was in the wrong spot.  Everything was in Arabic, and the barber was definitely not Brazilian. The guying getting his hair cut and the barber were both Middle Eastern and speaking what I assumed to be Arabic.  After I sat down, I couldn't really just get up and leave, so I decided to stay.

The barber was actually quite the character, he was wearing a white track suit and had one pant leg rolled up to his knee.  He was also wearing a sideways flat brim hat and had a very full beard.  However, he spoke enough Spanish so that I could tell him what I wanted.  Now, it didn't come out exactly how I wanted, but in the end it only cost 8 Euro.  Who can argue with an 8 Euro haircut?


Zuricalday


So just like the weeks before, I went to the Zuricalday bakery on Tuesday for half priced pastries.


  I had a little long John donut, but it was stuffed with pudding.  and then a "bollo de mantequilla" which means "butter bun".  Its a sweet bread with sugar on top and butter in between the two slices, but its not actually butter.  Its also egg whites, sugar, flour, and milk.  This is a very typical Basque pastry and you can't get it anywhere else in Spain.



Guggenhiem


On Wednesday, I had some time after class and I decided to stop by the Guggenhiem.  I have the 6 month membership and so it is free for me to go for the whole semester.


I really wish that I could show you guys pictures from inside with all the different exhibits, but they are pretty strict about photography.  There is at least one person in each room looking out to get you when you hold up your phone.

They just changed the exhibits in the Guggenhiem so it was great to see all the new stuff they have set up.


Thursday Night Adventures


So when I was running along the cliff in Getxo that goes along the bay, I noticed that there was this big pier down below.  The pier is at the very edge of the bay, and the cliff is probably 200 ft high, but there is a big switchback logging thing that leads to the water.  I thought it would be pretty cool to go out there and so I asked my friend Alex to go with me.

I really wish I had pictures to show you guys what it was like, but this is the best one I have right now.  I´m going to go back in the day light to show you guys a little better.



But anyways, so we started making our way down the switch back.  It was very large and beaten down. You could have easily driven a car down it, until we got to the second half.  The second part was much less worn, pretty muddy and about half the size. Then it suddenly stopped.  There was a pretty steep slippery rocky slope that we needed to go down. Luckily some one left a rope for us to use to get down.

Once we got to the pier, we realized that they were kind of like giant cinder blocks.  They were about 8 or 9 feet tall and about 15 or 20 ft wide.  Each one had two giant holes in the middle.  It would have been hard to get up on top, but people had left pieces of wood that we used as ramps and step ladders to get to the top.  The scariest part was shimmying down this skinny path. 


When we finally got on top, we walked to the end of the pier, avoiding those big holes along the way. At the end we were pretty far out into the ocean and the waves were big and splashing up against the rocks.  It was really peaceful!

Mall


The next morning was a no alarm kind of day, but I still woke up at 8 despite being up until two the previous night.  I spent the morning moping around and talking with Begoña about France.  At about 11:00 I headed out to go to the mall. 


There is actually two malls in Bilbao, one in the center of the city and one farther out.  I heard that the one farther out was cheaper and so I decided to check it out.


I went to this one store called New Yorker and I think it was the most entertaining.  I'm not sure if any one from that store has even been to the United States, let alone New York. They had all kinds of sports apparel with weird teams and bizzare English phrases as well.



Overall though the mall was great.  It was a little nostalgic and it made me miss home and hanging out at Woodfield.

Friday night


So later that night, I was watching the friendly between Spain and UK.  The announcers were speaking in Spanish, and so it is difficult enough to listen to them because they speak so fast, so when they mentioned the attacks in Paris, it went right over my head. 

I wouldn’t have known if my host mom wasn’t in the next room.  When she heard that, she whipped her head around and asked me in Spanish “Attacks in Paris??”.  So we switched to the news and watched everything unfold.  It was kind of scary because I knew so many people that were visiting Paris that weekend.  

There was 12 in Paris, and another one of my friends in Lourdes which is a southern city in France.  I immediately started texting everyone, and some of them didn't even know what happened.  I contacted everyone within an hour, but we kept talking for most of that night.  We were a little worried because France said they were going to close their borders, but everyone was able to return home without problems.


Talking to them the next few days were interesting.  We found out that about 5 of them were only a couple blocks away from the restaurant.  Most of my friends went and paid their respects.  They said that nearly everything was closed, and so they mostly just walked around and took in the city.  

Victoria


On Saturday, I went to Victoria for the day! Victoria is a relatively small city, but it is the capital of the Basque Country. 



We mostly spent the day walking around the city and just taking it all in.


Victoria was much more tranquil than Bilbao.  The buildings felt older and the city just felt like it was a little more historic and more pristine than Bilbao.  Bilbao tends to have a lot of modern developments that pop up everywhere.





We also went to the Cathedral de Santa María. There was hardly anyone inside and so we were basically alone.


I think my favorite part of this cathedral was the stained glass.  I think it might have been the time of day, but the stained glass was so impressive, I think it was the most impressive I have seen.  I just wish I could have captured that moment.  I just couldn't find an angle that would work with my camera.


In a way though, that kind of is a good thing, because no matter how many pictures you take, you never can capture anything perfectly and no one will fully understand that moment unless they were there.  Sorry about that mini rant right there,  I promise I won't try to be philosophical again.



Cathedral de Santa María



I don't know anything about these full building murals, but we did find a couple of them scattered around the city.


While we were walking around, we found a little museum.  It was only 1 Euro to enter and the guy working there was really nice.  He explained all of the different exhibits to us and talked to us for quite a while about some of the things they had there.

This fossil was 4 tall!


And these perfect cubes are actually minerals.


and so are these super long spike things!


Okay so when we stopped for gelato, this family all rolled up on their scooters.  It was pretty funny to see a full grown man riding a scooter.  But it was even funnier that he had an adult sized scooter. 

BUTTTT the funniest part was that on the dad's scooter there was a little black platform for his daughter to stand on while he was riding around. 



Sunday was a lazy day, I hung around the house, did some homework, talked with my family on Skype and hung out with Begoña.

Like I said, even though I didn´t go anywhere big, this week was still pretty eventful!

title: The First Couple Days
content:
So I successfully arrived in Bilbao and all is well! A lot has happened, and I will try to cover as much as possible!


After I arrived in the airport, I was picked up by my host mom and taken to her apartment.  She is a widow in her early sixties. She lives alone in a two bedroom two bathroom apartment in Algorta which is an area outside of Bilbao. Its about 30 minutes away by metro.  I have my own room and my own bathroom which is really nice, and from talking to the other students, it seems like a rarity.  I don't have any pictures of the apartment, but I will share those later.






So the next day, we went to the school and had an arrival presentation.  This covered things we should know about the city and the program and such.



After that, we all took a one hour placement test.  This was a little nerve racking because I needed to place into the 300 level in order to take the classes that I wanted.


While we are on the subject of classes, I can show you my schedule for this semester.  I will  be taking 13 credit hours.  So yah my schedule is reallyyy spread out.  Also, NO CLASS ON FRIDAY!!! That's never gunna happen again in my life!  All of the classes I will be taken will be exclusively taught in Spanish.  I will be taking a composition class, a linguistics class, a history class, and also a business internship class.  The internship will be at a company called RV Cooling. It is a Spanish company that makes industrial refrigerators.

Schedule!!




Later that day we were taken on a tour of the old town. We were shown quite a few different types of old Basque architecture and also explained the history of the town of Bilbao.  So I'll give you a quick crash course. First, Bilbao was a port city and a big hub of trading and commerce.  Then it became an industry hub.  It was one of the largest producers of steel in the world.  Lastly it transitioned to a more service based town. It has many companies in the tech industry.  One tour guide described it as a mini Silicon Valley.  There is also a lot of money in the tourist business because of the beautiful coast line and great fishing.  Bilbao is a part of the Basque region which is an area of Spain in the north.  The people here speak Basque, but also speak Spanish.  The region was very oppressed during the dictatorship under Franko, and many of the people are still very bitter about it.  Many would like to have independence from Spain.  In fact, one of my friends was confronted by someone who was upset that he was supporting the "enemy" by wearing a red and yellow Spanish jacket with the Spanish flag.  So yes, some people are pretty vocal about it.
Basque Flag

So lets talk about out tour now! First we went to the outskirts of the Bilbao area and saw the town of Plencia.  This was a fishing town way back in the Middle Ages, but it now it is very touristy. First we ate lunch at a country club that had a pool, tennis courts, and a jai alai court. When we were eating, I asked the tour guide (and later I found out he is the professor of two of my classes) about the jai alai court and if it was a popular game here.  He told me that jai alai was actually started in Basque country, so yes it is a popular sport here.  

In this picture you can see the traditional architecture of the houses and the church that is in the middle. We were told that these houses were owned by the rich.  They had built a wall around these houses and would use the church as a keep during attacks from the pirates.  Notice in the bottom left corner, the Basque flag that many people proudly fly.



Here you can see the river that runs through Plencia.  This river is actually an estuary, which means that it is like a river, except that it is connected to the ocean and its water levels vary with the tides.  



Next we went closer to the city and we saw one of the most ridiculous inventions I've ever seen.  So like I said, Bilbao is a port city, and so there are many large ships that come through.  The river is very wide and so drawbridges work, but they are slow and can get in the way of ships.  So they built this thing.  Its basically a hanging ferry boat.  The structure is tall enough so that large boats can go under, but cars can still get across by using the ferry.  Pedestrians can take elevators up and walk across the top of the bridge as well. There are only four still in existence and one of them is here in Bilbao.






Here is a video of the ferry going accross. I'm not sure if the video will work though.



















At the end of our trip we went outside of the city a little bit. We were able to see the beach that was by my house.  This picture also gives a good view of the actual city of Bilbao









Here are some of the houses that are really close to that beach.  They're pretty enormous for the area.







That last stop was the end of our tour and after that I went home and had some dinner with my host mom!  This post was very long winded and I don't think that the rest of them will be nearly as long or have nearly as many pictures as this one.  All is well with me right now and I am having a great time and learning a lot.  Already I can tell that I am improving with my Spanish.  I'm able to recognize my mistakes with tenses things like that.  Stay tuned for the next post about our tour of the inner city of Bilbao!

title: Pro tip: Don't Lose Your Passport
content:
So.  I had just arrived to Bilbao International Airport, I got my passport stamped and then met my host mom. We went home and unpacked and got ready to go out for pintxos (it’s the Basque word for tapas(tapas is the Spanish word for small dish or snack). When I was getting ready to leave, I decided that I should probably bring my passport just in case.  I couldn't find it though.  I wasn’t too worried because I figured it was somewhere in the room.

When we came back later that night I decided to dig around a little more.  I looked around the room and in my backpack and suitcase and pockets.  At that point I had to tell Begoña.  When I told her, she freaked out (I found out later that this is more her personality to do kinda over react a little, but at the time, it was the first day!) and I felt pretty terrible. We tore apart the room and all of my clothes and my backpack and my suitcase and the house and the car.  Nothing. 

This is when I panicked.  It also didn’t help that Begoña was freaking out too.  I spent a couple hours of that night searching info about my passport and figuring out what I needed to do. I reported my passport as lost or stolen and sent an email to the embassy asking for more information. The next morning I called the embassy, but I got an automated response telling me to visit the website. Classic.

Through my research I found that it was best for me to make a trip to Madrid to visit the embassy and request a new passport.  I signed up for the next available appointment; a Thursday morning in two weeks.

At this point I was upset I lost it, but I didn’t think that it was going to be that big of a deal.  I wasn't going to miss class because of the way my classes are set up, and I might be able to see a little bit of Madrid.  I was a little upset that I wasn’t going to be able to travel during a long 4 day weekend coming up in 3 weeks because the passport would take too long to process.  My friends were talking about going to London, but my passport wouldn't arrive until 4 weeks.

The very next day after I signed up for my appointment, my friend Matt showed me this email from the US travel office.  The email said that there were representatives coming from Madrid to Bilbao to deal with passport issues, on the very same day that I signed up for an appointment in Madrid.

YES!!! This was perfect!!! I would save time and money! Immediately I sent an email for the travel office asking to be given a time slot for when the representatives visit.  When I sent it I was told to get a response in about 3 business days.

Except it had been 6 days and I still heard nothing. Someone from the CIDE office told me that they were going to contact the embassy and see what was going on.

Then 2 hours later I received an email from the embassy! They told me that they sent me an email 3 days ago, but I know I definitely didn't get an email.  The email said that they would be able to give me a time slot on Wednesday morning at 9:00.

Perfect.  Now all I needed to do was get a passport photo.  There aren't any Walgreen's here to take your picture like in the states.  I spent about an hour searching on Spanish google and ended up finding a couple places that I think could do it.

The first store went okay. He took my picture, but they didn’t have the right size photos.  I tried to explain it to the guy, but I don't think he understood US passport photo requirements.  I paid for the large photo anyway and made my way to the next photo store. 

This guy was awesome.  He understood the special requirements and let me see the picture before he printed it. He printed two pictures, perfectly sized on one sheet of picture paper.

My appointment was at 9:00 AM the next morning, so I woke up at 6:30 so I could get there early.  Except I'm not a morning person so it ended up being 7:00.  I didn't end up leaving the house until 7:30 which is cutting it really close when the commute is about an hour.

I was opening the door to leave the apartment, I was running through a checklist in my head of the stuff I needed. Then I remembered if forgot to cut the pictures out!

I went into MacGyver mode. I didn't think I had ever seen any scissors in the house before.  I started opening drawers in the kitchen. I couldn't find anything.  I started contemplating using a knife to cut the paper.  Then I remembered that there was little scissors (I think they are used for nails or something) in the my bathroom drawer!

I rushed over and frantically cut out the pictures with these little baby nail scissors. It wasn't exactly straight, but it would have to do.

7:45. I was running to the metro. Anxiously I waited to get off and start booking it to the hotel where the embassy workers were.

The super nice hotel where the meeting was
I overestimated the time it would take to get there and I ended up 15 minutes early.  Except there was no one in the room where it was supposed to happen.  I waited until 9:05 (5 minutes after my appointment) and then I called a personal number that I had found on an email.  The woman answered and told me that she had "accidentally sent me the wrong time". Except she had sent me that appointment time 3 different times.  So I'm not sure what happened there
waiting room

She explained that my appointment was actually at 12:00.  I tried not to be too upset and I took the afternoon in full stride. I got coffee and a croissant from a local café and read the newspaper in Spanish.  Then I went across the street and spent 2 hours in the Guggenheim museum.

Tourists looking touristy

At 12:00 I finally had my meeting with the embassy and I had great news! First, they said my photo was fine, no problems there.  Second, they said that I was going to go on the London trip for sure.  They said that they could get me an emergency 1 year passport (valid for one year) to me in less that 4 days.  They also said that they can usually get me a 10 year passport in about 2 weeks, but it depends on how busy they are. 

After these long two weeks of research and emailing, it was so relieving to hear that I would be getting a passport so soon.  I'm not sure which one I will get yet, because they haven't updated me yet.  However, the next hurdle will be obtaining my student visa.  This was attached inside of my passport and the US embassy had no idea what to do and neither did my school.  I'm going to try and talk to someone in the city this week, so we will see how that goes. 


So morale of the story.  Don't lose your passport. But if you do, its not the end of the world, and the embassy can save your butt.

title: Krakow
content:
First off I´m sorry this post is so late! For once I had decent homework assignment and I was really caught up with that.

But anyways, this week was rainy and actually pretty cold.  I finally had to break out my peacoat.  I guess the weather fit the somber mood of the week as more and more information came out about the terrorist attacks.  Evidence of support was everywhere including the metro stop by my school.


I think that the weather has been throwing me off because it doesn't really feel like the seasons have changed and so I don't really feel like my semester should be almost over! However, like I said, this week was pretty cold and so I definitely noticed it. The people are really stingy on using water and electricity because its a lot more expensive than in the states. Its a little annoying, but it hasn't bothered me until this week when no one decided to turn on their heat.  The entire school was freezing so everyone was wearing their jackets in the classroom.  At home was the same thing, I had to wear two pairs of socks to be because my feet were so cold!

Internship

This was my final week at my internship.  I was enrolled in a class that placed us into a company where we would work for about 10 hours a week for 10 weeks. In addition to this we had 1 hour sessions where we would talk about our experiences and about the differences between Spanish business culture and American business culture.

It was an awesome experience and I wish I could work there more.  The actually assignments that I had were typical intern jobs, like putting away folders, entering business card data, relabeling boxes, and scanning documents. However, I did get to do some fun things, like in the beginning of the year I was making calls to tons of international companies.  I was basically asked to solicit, which was annoying to me, because I knew that I was going to annoy the other people, but it was actually pretty interesting.  I talked to companies from all over Europe (Norway, France, Germany, Netherlands, Croatia, Greece, Russia, Sweden, Switzerland, Poland, and tons of other countries).  Some times it was difficult to communicate with them because their English isn't the greatest, but we were always able to communicate.  

Aside from the actual work, just being in the company was the most beneficial thing.  I was able to experience the environment first hand.  I was able to talk with everyone there and meet the clients that came in.  I was able to see how international businesses work. Also, I was spending time with more native speakers which is always a good thing.  My boss, Susana helped me a ton with new words and pronunciation.  In turn I was able to help her with English!

All in all the internship class was awesome and I'm so glad that I was able to do that.


Random Things First 


So now real quick before we get into the weekend trip, I want to talk about a couple things. First off, the weekly pastry run! A "bollo de mantaquilla" with peanuts on top and then a croissant!



Secondly, since I have quite a decent metro ride (about 30 minutes one way and some times I go back and forth 4 times for a total of 2 hrs) I always try and find a way to use that time.  Usually, I'm stuck standing so I can't type my essay or blog, I can't write notes or postcards.  when I'm standing I usually read my Europe in the World book or the newspaper, or I'll watch a movie or TV show on my phone. I have probably been doing too much of the later. Anyways, this week I decided to watch Schindler's List only because it always appears on the "Top Movies of All Time" lists.  So when I started watching it and realized that it was about Krakow, I almost pooed myself because it was so relevant.  (Side note: the movie is amazing and definitely lives up to the hype)


Also another random thing, the day of our flight I wanted to by snacks for traveling and ended up buying these ketchup and mustard puff things.  I only bought it because it was weird, but they ended up being pretty good! They are kind of like the Pirates Booty things we have in the US, with the flavor of ketchup and mustard.




Krakow


So waayyyy back in the first weeks of school, we were deciding where we wanted to travel too.  My friend Matt threw out the idea of going to Krakow to see the Auschwitz museum.  I had never heard of Krakow at the time, but Auschwitz kind of jumped out at me as somewhere that I wanted to go.  

In the weeks before I started doubting the trip.  Do I really want to go to such a depressing place? The city is probably going to be boring. Should I have gone somewhere else? Nevertheless, this trip was one of my favorites.  

So I kind of started the trip off on a bad foot.  I had to take the metro into the city to catch the bus to the airport, but immediately after I stepped off the metro, I realized that I had forgotten my passport in my house.  I had to return home, but I wasn't going to have enough time to take the metro back to Bilbao.  So I had to bite the bullet and pay a 30 Euro taxi to the airport instead of a 2 Euro bus.  However, I made it to my flight with plenty of time.

We were traveling pretty far and since Bilbao isn't that big of an airport we had to have a connection flight from Munich.


It turned out to be pretty nice.  It was a good little break and stretch our legs.  Also, they had free coffee machines that made cappuccinos, lattes, hot chocolate, tea, espresso and everything in between, so that was fun!


We arrive in Krakow pretty late, at about 12:00 so as soon as we landed, we went to the hostel and went to bed. 


The next morning, we went downstairs to have the free breakfast that the hostel offered and we were blown away.  This free breakfast was amazing by anyone's standards let alone a free hostel breakfast.  There was bacon, salami, chorizo, tons of cheeses, cereal, crepes, toast, yogurt, eggs, and juice. It was a great way to start the day.


 Over breakfast we decided that today we were going to go on a couple of the free walking tours.  The first one was going to be of the old town and the second was through the Jewish ghetto.  Our tour guide was a history major and gave an excellent tour. I'm just going to high light some things from the tour and also some photos I took along the way.








I'm just going to high light some things from the tour.  So Krakow used to be the capital city as well as a very important trading city. They had this one, which they used for food and livestock and day to day things.  But the vendors who sold more expensive things like gold, silk gems, spices and furs didn't want to be by the smelly local market.  So they built two squares. One for luxury goods and one for day to day things.


This building right here is called the Cloth hall and is one of the old trading locations.  Nowadays, its mostly just a place for tourists to spend money.



Here's a photosphere that I took from the side of this building so you can get a better view.

Main Square Photosphere

Also in that photosphere, you might have seen this tower.  This is the Town Hall Tower and its actually leaning over a little bit.  Wayyyy back when, there used to be a whole town hall and a grainery attached to this tower.  Then in the 20th Century they destroyed the grainery but left the rest of the town hall.  But they messed up when during the demolition and broke the foundation of the city hall.  So then they had to destroy that too! But then when they were destroying city hall, they didn't realize that the city hall tower was leaning up against it.  So they had to reinforce the tower so it didn't fall.


This next picture is a model of the old grainery and town hall.  The square building is the grainery and the triangular part is the city hall and then the tower is obviously what is left there today.


On the other side of the main plaza was this giant cathedral called St. Mary's Basilica.  It was originally build in the 13th century, but during the Mongol invasion it was burned down.  However it was reconstructed because they thought that Krakow was too important. Every hour there is a trumpet player who plays a little song that was actually a signal, but the signal gets cut off suddenly at the end to commemorate the 13th century trumpeter that was shot in the throat with an arrow while playing the signal.


St. Mary's Basilica Photosphere

We ended our tour at the Wawel Castle.  It built up on a hill in the 13th century, but it was also burned down by the Mongols.  They rebuilt in the 14th Century along with this church.  This church is pretty famous in Poland and there is a ton of famous people buried here.



Here is the dragon of Krakow. Well I guess its actually a statue.


 There is a legend that says that there was a dragon that would terrorize the land, killing people and burning the villages.  The only way to stop him was to sacrifice a virgin woman. Many men tried to kill the dragon but none could.  Soon there was no women left to sacrifice expect for the kings daughter, He said that any man who kills the dragon could marry his daughter.  So a shoemaker came up with a plan to feed the dragon a lamb stuffed with sulfur.  The dragon got very thirsty and drank all of the water from the river.  He drank so much that the dragon exploded. So the shoemaker married the daughter and they lived together in peace. 



Our tour ended pretty far away from the city center and we had to get back in order to meet up for the second tour of the day.  We really wanted to get some real polish food, but we didn't have time so we went to a kebab place instead.  Surprisingly good food though and super cheap! it was like $3 and it filled me up!



 Our second tour of the day was of the Jewish ghetto.  The tour started off and the guide gave us a little history on the town of Kazimierz.  He told us that the town was created by the King Kazimierz III (cleverly named after himself). The King allowed for his Queen's people ( the Jews to come to Poland and many went to Kazimierz.  It was sort of like a haven for them.


During the war they were crowded into a part of the town of Kazimierz which is now colloquially called the Jewish Ghetto. Many families were forced into small apartments, sometimes 4 families in one.  But that was only temporary until they were sent to concentration camps.  There were 65,000 Jews that lived here, but after the war there were only 500. 




Our tour guide eventually brought us to on the film sites for the Schindler's List.  It was cool to see that only days after seeing the movie.  The guide told us that the ghetto was in really bad shape up until a few years ago.  Kazimierz was turned into alternative housing after the war and was a rough neighborhood until the 2000's.  After Schindler's List came our, the Jewish Ghetto started to become a tourist attraction and so the town began to redevelop.



I'm sorry, I was tired and I didn't pay attention to what this cathedral was about, but it was really pretty at night!  but it really wasn't night, it was more like 4:30. The sun sets early in Krakow.


After our tour we went to go see Schindler's factory.  Even though the last tour already passed, it was cool to see it.


We decided to grab buy one of the snacks that the tour guide recomended.  Its called Zapiekanka and pronounced like its spell. Its basically just pizza on a long bread.




It was pretty hard to eat, and so it made for a great photo op.



Thanks Lauren for the great faces!


After our snack we went to the hostel where they served us a free dinner.  The dinner was provided by a local restaurant and it was fantastic!!




Auschwitz


 So the next morning we woke up pretty early to catch the bus to Auschwitz and it took about 1.5 hours to get there.  When we got off it was cold and drizzling. We had a 6 hour tour of the whole complex.  It sounds really long, but it was definitely necessary.  Anything shorter and you would miss so much. We spend 3 hours in Auschwitz I and 3 hours in Auschwitz II (Bercanau).  In general, the tour was a hard thing to describe.  It was incredible, but sobering to see everything first hand.


"Arbeit macht frei"  which is German for "Work makes your free". A most obvious lie.



The buildings in are almost all original, although some are remodeled on the inside to show the exhibits.







Some of the bunks that they lived in.  There would be sometimes up to 5 in a bed.


Later on we were able to visit one of the gas chamber sites.


This is where they would have roll call. This was usually a pretty terrible time for the prisoners.  Sometimes they would keep them outside for up to 19 hours.  Also, keep in mind that they temperatures here get well below zero and all they had for clothing was basically a thin long sleeved tshirt and thin cotton pants. 


This is called the Black Wall were many executions took place.  They built the black wall to prevent the bullets from damaging the brick behind it.


Another powerful part of the museum, was the children's drawings of the events.




This is the Book of Names.  It has 4.2 million names of Holocaust Victims.  The book was enormous. Probably 7 feet tall and 30 ft long.



After we finished in the Auschwitz I camp we stopped for lunch and then headed to Auschwitz II


Personally, I thought the second half of the tour was much more impactful. As soon as we got to Auschwitz II - Bernkenau, we were taken up the main guard tower.  


From here we could see everything.  I felt like the barracks went on forever.





This was the bathroom there.  It was actually a really good place for the prisoners.  The toilets were public, but the officers usually didn't follow them in and so the prisons could plan escapes.  Also, the people who emptied the toilets had an great job. They were able to work under a roof and they were generally unsupervised.  Because their clothes were smelly, the officials wouldn't want to talk to them and so they stayed away. This allowed them to smuggle documents and things from outside underneath their clothes.  Because they brought waste outside of the camp, they could have contact with the outside world (perhaps a local farmer or villager)


This is a replication of the in side of one of the barracks. About 700 people in each barracks and usually 5 to a bed.


A daily itinerary would look like this:

Woke up. Went to bathrooms. Had small coffee. Went to roll call. Went to work. Had a liter of soup. Back to work. Then roll call again. Then they got some bread. Went to sleep.


Again, walking through here it felt like the barracks went on forever.



Here is a photo of what was left of one of the gas chambers.





This is where their clothes would be washed.  The building was shaped like a U. They would put the, in on this side.  And then walk to the bottom of the U, where they would have their head shaved,  number tattooed, and take an extremely cold shower. Then they would go up the other side of the U and pick up their clothes.


This rubble is what used to be a gas chamber before the Germans destroyed it before surrendering.


Right next to that gas chamber is the Auschwitz Memorial



At the end of the tour they had wall and wals of photos and stories about the people who died.  A lot of the time its hard to relate and the people become figures and statistics. Like Joseph Stalin said "One death is a tragedy; one million is a statistic".  These photos help to humanize them.



After the tour I also took this photosphere more or less in the middle of the camp.   I think it kind of helps to understand how big it was.

Auschwitz II Photosphere

All in all the tour was great.  I think that it was a good thing to see and especially when I am so close.  It was crazy to me how big the camps were at Auschwitz.  And then to think about how small Auschwitz was compared to the entire war.  Its just so hard for us to wrap our minds around the size of the whole operation.

After our time in Auschwitz, we went back to Krakow and went out to eat.  We stopped at a place that our tour guide had recommended called Babci Maliny which translates to Strawberry Grandmother.


The restaurant we really nice and it definitely felt like Grandma's house!


There was even a guy playing piano!


So to eat we had Zurek soup which is like a sourdough soup.  It was thick and super tasty.

\

Next of course we had lots of pierogies!



The food was awesome and it was ridiculously cheap! We bought 5 plates of pierogies and 3 bowls of soup for about $35!

The next morning I got up early to get one last view of the city with Kelsey. We mostly just walked around and took pictures.



We went into that giant basilica on the main square, but there was no picture taking allowed. I'm truly sorry for that because the inside was amazing. I've seen a lot of cathedrals by now, but this one was much different.  The decoration inside was incredibly detailed.  I did however take a discrete selfie of the ceiling for you guys to enjoy.


This week we saw a ton of these little stands selling these pretzels things so we decided to try them.


It was less of a pretzel and more of a bread circle and it tasted amazing, so for 25 cents, it was a steal!


They don't use Euro here the use zloty.  I thought it was funny that each bill had a different geometric shape on it.


Oh, and of course before we left we picked up some Paczkis to eat in the airport.


Getting back home was quite the adventure though.  The flights out of Krakow were delayed and so we arrived to Munich an hour late and missed our connection to Bilbao.  We thought that we would just get on the next flight that was in an hour, but it was full.


So they sent us to Frankfurt and from there we were going to go to Bilbao.  Except the flight from Munich to Frankfurt was also delayed!! Our flight to Bilbao was leaving in 10 min, after we arrived in Frankfurt.  Before we got off, we decided that we were going to do every man for himself, don't wait for anyone just run to the plane.  So here we are 4 frantic Americans sprinting down the airport.  It was actually pretty far away, it was 40 gates away and it took me about 8 minutes to get there.  I was panting and sweating because I was wearing my winter coat, but I made it in time, and so did everyone else!

If anything the nice thing was that we were flying with Lufthansa.  It was a little bit bigger seats and some more leg room.  The best part was that they gave you a sandwich and two drinks on every flight! Even the 30 minute flight from Munich to Frankfurt!


So finally at 11:40 PM we landed in Bilbao.  But wait that was a problem too because the last bus from the airport to the city center leaves at 11:45 PM and I was not going to pay ANOTHER 30 Euro taxi.  So again we are sprinting through the airport.  Alas we made it on time for the bus and we all made it home on time.


For those of you who made it this far, congratulations, there was a lot of text in the blog and not so many fun pictures. Again, my apologies for taking so long to write this! I was really busy with a paper last week.  I'm going to try and make it up to you by finishing the next weeks blog today...but don't count on it!

title: Half Way Point
content:
So I am just about half way through my semester already! Its has gone by incredibly quickly so far! In general, life has started to slow down and things have become much more normal.  So day to day life has slowed down

I've definitely seen my Spanish level increase. I am much more comfortable speaking with native speakers.  I often still make grammar mistakes and I take some time to conjugate words in my head, but I am thinking about the rules instead of just ignoring them.  

Something weird has been happening with my writing recently.  I am making a lot more spelling mistakes than I used to.  I often forget to put "h" in "hecho" or "hemos" ( the "h" in Spanish is not pronounced and so this is a common spelling mistake, but I never used to have this problem). In high school when I wrote in Spanish, I would think of the Spanish word that I wanted and then write it.  Now I think that because I have been speaking and listening a lot more than writing and reading, that I am associating the verbs and nouns with sounds instead of whole words.  Not sure if this is a thing, I'm just a science person trying to understand Psychology.

Skype Interview 


On Wednesday, I had a my first Skype interview.  It was difficult for me to find a good location to do it.  I wanted to do it at school, because I felt like the WiFi would be best there, but the interview was at 7:30 PM here and so I was afraid that the classrooms would be closed.  I tried to get a group study room at the library, but they wouldn't let me because I wasn't a normal student.  So I ended up having to do at home.  I wanted privacy, but at the same time a good location.  I used my room and moved all the furniture around and took the paintings off the wall so that I could get a nice white background.  It was quite a hassle, but it turned out pretty good in the end.

Gurnika and Mundaka 


This Friday, we had another little trip that was sponsored by our study abroad program.  We went to the towns of Gurnika and Mundaka for a day. Before this trip I didn't know what Gurnika was or what had happened there, so I'll fill you guys in. 

Basically during the Spanish Civil War, the old dictator Franco, gave the ok to Mussolini and Hitler to target Gurneka in order to overthrow the Basque Government. Gurneka is a town of about 5,000 with absolutely no military developments.  The dropped large explosive bombs and well as incendiary bombs.  After the bombing, gunships would shot the people who were escaping the burning city. 1,654 civilians were killed.


We went through the Guernica Peace Museum and saw many photos of the destruction and learned more about the attacks and the Spanish Civil War.


Gurnika is also a big center for the Basque Government. Is where the Biscayan (Biscaya is a providence of Basque Country) government has met for centuries.  We went to the Meeting House where they have these meetings.  The history of the meetings around the Tree of Gernika.  The original tree was planted in the 14th Century and they keep planting new ones after the only one dies. 


To call the counsel, they used to have 5 people sound horns on 5 different mountain peaks.  The first horn would come from Gernika and then the next one would be a few towns over and then the next town and then the next one.  The tour guide had a horn thing and we got to try it ourselves.  As you can see I wasn't very good at it...




We also went inside the Meeting House and saw where they sit and the main corridor. They had a beautiful stained glass window with a depiction of each town around the edge of it.


That windmill in the middle represents Getxo, that where I live!


 We met up with a woman and started a little walking tour. First we went to the Church of Santa Maria de la Antigua.  It was a very pretty church!



This church was a very popular place for people to stop while on el Camino de Santiago.  Many times they would stay up top in the gallery.  I don't remember what is was called, sorry! The tour guide even let us go up there! It was pretty cramped, but it was really high! 


There also was a funny little door you used to go up there.



Oh yah, I took a photosphere here!

Photosphere inside Church of Santa Maria

After our tour, we headed over to the town square to get lunch!



After our lunch we went to Mundaka, which is a small port town that has a biosphere reserve.  It is also a world renown surfing location because the waves come from the left. 


The town was super pretty and it was a great place to just walk around and take in all the views.



I'm really not sure how I balanced like this
 I also took a couple Photospheres here!

Mundaka Photosphere 1

Mundaka Photosphere 2

San Juan


On Saturday a few of us headed over to San Juan. This is one of the places that all the locals say that you have to visit.  I definitely agree, its an amazing place and it helped that the weather was amazing. To get here we had to ride a bus for about an hour and then we had about an hour hike to get to the base of the island/mountain thing.


It was a beautiful walk along the coast and through the country side.




Like I said the views are just amazing.






This journey was incredible.  There is a legend that says that if you ring the bell in the church three times, you get a wish, but unfortunately the church was closed.  I also took two photospheres, one at the top and one at the bottom!

Photosphere San Juan Top

Photosphere of San Juan Bottom


Sunday Hike

I went on another hike with hiking group.  Even though its not really a hike, its more like a trek, because its not really a hike.  It is much harder than any hike that I have ever been on, but at the same time its not climbing. We don't pull out ropes and start repelling off cliffs.  This hike was a little bit farther away, but I definitely enjoyed this one much more.  The mountain was beautiful and the scenery was amazing as well.  It also didn't rain.  I think that helped a lot.




I took this picture awesome picture, and we weren't even half way up yet!





Also a photosphere that I took from the middle!

Photosphere Urkiola


I loved how the trees just blended in with the rocks.  The guy in charge, Paul, explained to us that when the trees get cut down, they branch out and move around the cut.  So that why they get that octopus shape.


As you can see, this part of the hike was fairly steep!


So this is a Cairn. Its just a pile of rocks, but it is a way point for travelers ( in this case us! the hikers! ) to follow.


Again, this is not your average hike, it was basically a little bit of climbing at this point.  I think everyone was on all fours at one point.


Like I said, I loved this hike the most and this was one of the reasons why.  The forest was just so beautiful.  The moss cover rocks looked amazing.


Finally we reached the very top! It was pretty hard to take pictures from here just because of how big everything was, so I think the best way to look at it is with the photosphere.  It just makes the panoramas much less distorted and real.



At the top I took two photospheres from two different locations. I think the second one is better because there isn't as many clouds so you can see much farther!

Photosphere of Urkiola Peak 1

Photosphere of Urkiola Peak 2


We stopped at the top and had lunch and then made our way back down.


The whole hike took about 7 hours, but we did take quite a few breaks.  It was about 7 miles long and we climbed up 2000 ft.  It was a pretty good day!

So just after this, I have a little sections on interesting things that I've been noticing.  Sorry this post has been so late, I need to step up my game and get these rolled out on Monday or Tuesday again!

Interesting Things


Weird Folders

The folders here are different than the US.  When I received my Deusto information packet on the first day, I thought that the folder was just special and they wanted to look flashy for all the new students. Its like a manila folder with folds to make sure the papers don't fly out the side and then elastic to make sure it stays shut. However, when I went to the stores, this was the only type available.  I just assumed that something like a folder would be more of a universal thing.


 Long Vacations

This isn't just a Spain thing, this is more of an all of Europe thing.  The people here get much more vacation time, about 25 to 30 days in most countries.  That's in addition to national holidays!  Usually this vacation time is used in August and so that is the really busy tourist month in Europe.

Stick Deodorant? Who needs it??

I started to run out of deodorant and so I started looking around at the shops and stores, I couldn't find my deodorant.  I expected to see familiar brands, but that wasn't the case at all! There was barely any selection and the stuff that was there was all that weird liquid deodorant.  I couldn't find a single stick type deodorant.  I ended buying that liquid kind. I had doubts about how well it would work, but so far it is working out

title: Long Weekend in London
content:
This week was a little busy for me with school and applications and errands and such. I had my first actual paper.  But don't freak out because it was in English and only one page long.

A Few things from this week


Just like my mom at home, I end up helping Begoña with technology.  In the past I have helped her redownload Farmville on her tablet and find songs on her phone.  This week I helped her update her laptop to windows 10 and reconfigure her WiFi repeater.  She calls me "un artista", or an artist.  I like that I can help her and return the favor for all that she does for me.

Its impossible to print here! You have to go to a computer and sign into your account in the printer settings.  You have to send it to a certain printer.  Then you have to go up two floors and go into another room.  Then put money on your ID Card and use this credit card machine thing next to the printer to activate it.  Then turn the printer on and change some settings. Then login on the printer and find your print job and then FINALLY you get to print.  Its quite the process and I'm glad that my friend Jill was able to just show me how to do it instead of trying to figure it out.  She told me it took her two hours to print the first time!!


London Trip



Our trip to London started in Plaza Moyua in Bilbao. We took a 30 min bus to the airport and made it to the gate with an hour to spare.  But our flight was delayed almost 2 hours.  Go figure. Classic Spanish thinking to be very lax with punctuality.  Regardless, we finally boarded the plane and we headed off to London!



I couldn't quite capture this midair sunset, but take my word that it was great
Once we landed in Gatwick airport, we had to take a train to the city because it is so far away. Then from there we took the tube ( its what they call the subway) to our hostel.  We had a room all to ourselves with our own bathroom and shower.  Everything appearing pretty clean, so the sleeping situation was pretty good!


We woke up at the crack of dawn and had breakfast at a super awesome family owned cafe.


What else can you order in London besides a full English Breakfast??


Here is the tube station that was really close to our hostel.  The tube stations are pretty hectic and a lot more confusing than Bilbao or Chicago. There are many different lines and usually 3 or 4 levels in every station.  Luckily, Adriana has international data and so we were able to use the Internet to look up a lot of things.





 The second stop in the morning was the Parliament Building, but we didn't stop for long. We basically stopped just to see it and take pictures. And there was enough time for me to take a Photosphere!  There was tons of really nice cars going in and out constantly. 

Buckingham Palace Photoshere



Second stop was the Borough Market, which is basically a more permanent farmers market. This was pretty fun! We hung around for about an hour and tried different foods, and pastries, and teas.  


The chefs of the group were very impressed

I also tried watermelon juice.  It wasn't that good, it was basically mashed up watermelon.


Next we took a short walk over to see London's Bridge, you know, to see if it was falling down. It wasn't.


The bridge was actually very underwhelming.  It was just a normal bridge. 


I thought it was really funny that all the taxis look like they are stuck in the 1940s


We went to the Tower of London next.  Its basically a reallllllllly old castle that is right on the river.




From the Castle you can see the Tower Bridge.  


Tower of London Photosphere


 Some ancient graffiti in the castle


Look at the size of this book!!! The title was "Understanding Women". Nahhhhh I'm just kidding, it was for keeping trading records.


 At this point in the day we were starving and so we saw this food truck close by and ate here.



Tower Bridge was next.  This was one of the things I was most excited for.  It looks really cool and its a really old draw bridge andddd there was a glass floor in the walkway!


Tourist being touristy with their selfie sticks


Hey! Those are my feet!


Don't worry, we didn't use a selfie stick, so we were being socially acceptable.


Also when we were up on the bridge, there just so happened to be a boat that was passing through.  So then we got to see the bridge lift!



The views up in the bridge were incredible! I wish we could have spend more time up there!


After going up the bridge we were able to see the engine room and it was AWESOME!! I could have spend a couple hours there.


Next stop is a big one for a lot of people.  Platform 9 3/4.  There was a 30 min line, and there was professional photographers there working, but we were able to take our own pictures for freee! I just couldn't do this picture very well, so focus more on the group photo.





Abbey Road was next on the list. This was a great adventure, possibly one of my favorites.  This intersection is actually pretty dang hard to find.  We walked for probably a hour in multiple different directions.  But in the end, we eventually found it! Sorry that its dark!  The sunsets in London reallly early. Like 6:00.  So we had no idea that it would be this dark when we planned our day.

One of the best parts of this spot is that the street is still fully functioning and the crosswalk is not part of an intersection and so the cars get mad when you hold up traffic just to take a picture.

After this superrrr long day, we went to a pub and had a bite to eat before another busy day.


We woke up bright and early the next morning and had our breakfast in the hostel.  They provided a simple breakfast ( cereal, toast, coffee) for about $1.50.


First stop of the second day was the London Natural History Museum.  It was free and we mostly went in to see the dinosaurs.




After that, we headed off to Westminster Abby.  Some of the tunnels to get to the tube are really long.  This one was almost a half a mile!


Egg and bacon sandwich for a snack from a metro store


I also got this skittles drink because I had never seen it before.  It was a huge let down.  Its basically just strawberry milk.


So here is Big Ben!! He lives right next to Westminster Abby so we saw him on the way.

The Abbey, for those of you who don't know is a big cathedral where they do tons of Royal weddings and coronations.  There is also a ton of famous people buried here like Isaac Newton and Charles Darwin.  We were not able to take photos here, but I snuck a few in just for you guys.

Also the building is not curved, it was just to dang tall so I had to take a vertical panorama and it got a little smushed.





After the tour, I took a quick Photosphere just outside of the Westminster Abbey.

Westminster Abbey Photosphere

We were all starving at this point, so we went to find somewhere to eat lunch.


When you're in London, you have to ride a double decker bus right?


I had to stop and take a picture for the fans.


Lunch was great and it was relatively low price.  It was only about $15

Appetizer was fried fish thing.

Main course was chicken with  cous cous


After a hefty meal we headed over to the London eye.  It kind of a cool structure.  There is only two giant posts on one side that hold it up. It looks like it should fall because there are no supports on the other side.  In order to keep it from tipping, there are cables that go from the hub to the ground.  I was promptly made fun of when I started talking about how it was interesting that there were only two parts in compression ( three if you count the bottom of the Ferris wheel ) because it is held together mainly by cables. 


You can see these cables better in this picture. They are in the upper left and continue off the picture.


The top of this thing gave ups some great opportunities for pictures and I got some excellent panoramas!




After another long day, everyone was ready to eat and relax a little.  We were also kind of sick of how expensive the food was here.   So instead of going out again, we decided to make our own food.   The two chefs of the group (Matt and Patricia) were very excited to finally get to cook The hostel had a kitchen that we were allowed to use, 




There was no meat at the store, so we had a vegetable fried rice, and it was very good!!



So I wanted to get out and see the scenery of the United Kingdom, and so I planned a trip to Dover.  Its on the southern tip of the UK and about an hour bus ride from London.  We had two stops in mind; Dover Castle and the White Cliffs of Dover.


To get to the Castle, we had to hike up the hill that it was on and so that took about 20 min.


When we finally arrived, the views were breathtaking.  This castle wasn't the most beautiful thing ever, but I loved how rugged and real looking it was.



Uh oh, we got a couple of punks over here!


With our ticket we got to have a couple tours.  Ironically they weren't for the castle, but instead for a war sites.  The first was of the war tunnels.  These were originally dug out in the Napoleonic war in the 1700s. 2000 soldiers lived, slept and ate here.  Later in World War I it was deemed unfit for humans and they used it mostly for storage.  


A lot of this tour was about the big rescue mission of  Dunkirk, where over 300,000 British and French soldiers were evacuated to Dover to escape the advancing Nazi army.  The tour was very well done with interesting videos and historic recreation of the control rooms and switch boards and telegraph repeaters.  This next picture is from just outside the tunnels where they jut out of the white chalky cliffs.


The next tour was of the underground hospital.  The built this hospital, expecting many casualties in WWII, but they didn't have nearly any at all and so it went generally unused.  


We weren't supposed to take pictures, but I did anyways.  Just you lovely people.  One funny story we heard was about the air tubes they used for sending messages around the hospital ( the tubes are like the ones at Walgreen's where they shoot medicine to you next to your car window).  They said that if you heard someone screaming in the hospital, it wasn't because someone was in pain, it was because one of the nurses was playing a prank and shot a dead rat through the tube and onto someones desk.


Fun fact: This is the first ever anti aircraft gun ever built.  It was build in 1917.  Dover was being bombed up to 10 times a day.  So they created this gun which shoots little pieces of flak (little pieces of metal) into the air.  With a few guns, you can make a sort of wall of metal debris which will wreck airplanes engines.  So because of this the airplanes will turn away instead of risking damage.  This brought the number of bombings down to zero per day.


I also took a Photosphere nearby this artillery spot.

Dover Artillery Photosphere

After they shot of some blank rounds, we headed into the main part of the castle.  This castle doesn't have much historical elements inside.  Most are in a museum, and so nearly all of the stuff was interactive. It was actually really fun.  I felt like a little kid again.


ready for battle




You always need to be on the lookout for assassins



Once we finally reached the top, the views were amazing! You could see so far!


Here you can see that the castle grounds included so much more than just the keep.


That church like building in the middle is the oldest building on the grounds and I believe is was about a century old.


We walked out onto the castle grounds and I took this beautiful photo along with an excellent Photosphere.



 Dover Castle Grounds Photosphere

After a long day at the castle, we decided we needed to have tea time. After all, we were in Britain!


The final stop on the list was the white cliffs! I was very excited about this! We took a little boat tour out into the bay where we got a great view of the white cliffs. We were really lucky with the weather and how sunny it was!

waiting for the tour the little harbor side shack




After the tour we grabbed a quick dinner and headed back home.  I was really excited that we got to board the plane from the tarmac! I had never been able to do that before and it was kinda fun!


In short London was very fun. We did tons of things and had very little sleep.  I loved everything that we did and I think London is an amazing town and Great Britain is definitely somewhere I will visit again.  I loved the culture and how that meshed with the modern world.  I think that London did a much better job that Madrid at doing that.  I'm going to put up a little video recap of this trip too, but I didn't have time to finish it yet and I really just want to get this blog posted because it is already Friday!

So after that ridiculously long blog, I just have a few interesting things that I noticed this week.

Interesting Things


No Central Air

I'm not sure how different this is, or how much they are used here, but I have seen it in a few places. Instead of having central air, they just have this small heater in the ceiling. 


Two Faucets

I have no idea why they use two faucets, one is for hot and one is for cold. So you either burn your hands, or you get hypothermia.  Its really a dumb system and I saw it pretty frequently in the UK.


Keep Left?

It was funny to see the keep left sign in the metro because I'm so used to everything being on the right!  In the streets the had words on the ground to remind you which way to look for traffic.  I assume that because people get in accidents because they forget that they drive on the wrong side of the road.

title: Road Tripping to Portugal
content:
Okay, so I obviously didn't get this blog out as fast as I wanted to and I sincerely apologize.  That one essay really kinda of threw me for a loop.  I also have another big essay coming so fair warning the blog for the next weekend will definitely be late as well. Any ways, lets get on and talk about things!
So I don´t think I ever really documented the inside of my university buildings, so here are a couple of pictures of that!

This is the main hall way that runs through the main part of the school.


Then we have two large courtyards that have palm trees inside of them.  They have a plastic roof over the top, but it still gets pretty cold inside the courtyards.



Thanksgiving




So I am not someone to get home sick, like I never get homesick.  However, I knew that Thanksgiving was going to be one of those days.  Even during the week building up to Thanksgiving I was feeling homesick. 

On Thanksgiving our study abroad office put on a Thanksgiving dinner for all of us, which was super nice of them.  A few weeks before Itziar (one of the teachers) sent out an email asking people if they would like to help out on a little Thanksgiving committee.  I thought we would help organize or give sugestions for food or something, so I decided to help out, but I wasn’t able to make the meeting time because I had class.  So she said I could stop by her office after class one day, but I forgot to go. Whooooops!

Even though I didn’t go they planned a pick up touch football game for before the dinner and they probably did other things, but I didn't hear about them and I don't know exactly because I didn't go!.  Is any Thanksgiving truly an American Thanksgiving without a little football before? Everyone was pretty excited about this. 

A few days later, I was walking out of class and one of my teachers said to me “I can’t wait to hear your speech!” I kinda was confused and I didn’t really think anything of it. Then the next day, I was talking with one of my friends and she said “So I hear you’re giving a speech?” I was kind of taken a back and said “What are you talking about?” She replied “Ya! Itizar (the organizer) was talking about it in class today”. So at this point I was a little freaked out. I sent her an email asking about the speech situation, and she replied “Yup, you’re giving a speech!”

I don’t really know why I didn’t back out of it, but for whatever reason I decided to go with it. I didn’t have time to write anything before because I had a pretty big paper that was due the day before.  So I wrote it on the metro ride to dinner.  But hey!  It went pretty well, I didn’t go with the script, but I didn’t make a fool of myself!

So actually before I gave that speech, we had our little game of football.  It actually wasn’t that little though! I think about 30 something people showed up, so we had two games of 7 on 7 going. The study abroad office rented out one of the turf soccer fields. It was raining, but it was still a ton of fun!!

So now dinner! We went to a really nice restaurant.  The teachers and host families were telling us to dress really nicely, but I didn’t exactly pack a suit and tie.  But I was totally fine with jeans and a button down. 

 Oh and they had some excellent food! I wouldn’t say that it was Thanksgiving food, but it was a good shot.

First dish was a pumpkin vegetable puree (with bread of course)

Second dish was turkey! It was a kind of small portion and not nearly as much as I would normally have on Thanksgiving

For dessert, we were promised a "Pumpkin Pastry".  I was pretty pumped because this meant pumpkin pie to me.  That was a stupid over sight on my part because we are in Spain and of course it will be different.  The actual dessert was pumpkin sherbet, a brownie, and some pumpkin marmalade on the side.

Oh and there was a photo booth!


There was no brothers or parents or aunts or uncles or grandmas or grandpas or cousins or spaetzle or stuffing or pumpkin pie or mashed potatoes or gravy, but it was a pretty decent Thanksgiving anyways.

Bakery


One day a couple of my friends were talking to our professor for Europe in the World class (this is the same prof that was frantically waving to me from across the parking lot at the beginning of the semester) about cooking and pastries and bread.  Eventually they came up with this idea that Jose (the professor) was going to bring them to a bakery to show them how they bake the bread.  I wasn’t totally in the conversation because a lot of it went over my given my ramen noodle and easy mac level of cooking, but nevertheless I kinda nudged myself into being able to tag along as well!


So on Friday, we met up at a bakery in the Old Town of Bilbao.  Jose is kind of a nut about bread and so apparently he makes friends with bakers because goes there so often and he just likes to talk to them about the bread.  So we went inside and he showed us the different breads and explained the different curing techniques and the ovens and the preparation and basically everything in between.


It smelled amazing, the bread was delicious and it was definitely worth the trip out there




Road Trip!



After the bakery, we made our way to go pick up the car for the weekend. The woman ended up giving us a free upgrade to from our little two door Ford to a BMW crossover (also, I only said crossover to annoy my mom).  It was a really fun drive.  The steering was tight, the (engine) had a great pull, there was plenty of room in the back, and it got great gas mileage (picture of the car later on!) . Our first destination was Salamanca! 





We stopped and walked around the city for a little bit.  We saw the Plaza Mayor and took some time to get tapas at one of the bars for a little dinner.

Plaza Mayor de Salamanca

Oh that middle thing is actually a semi fried egg yoke, but it was really good!



Saw one of the most bizarre street sweepers there that looked exactly like Nu-Nu the vacuum from Teletubbies.

Later we just walked around and explored the city to see some of the buildings and the cathedral



And we also wandered back to plaza mayor again to see it lit up at night

After Salamanca, I took the wheel and we headed for Porto, Portugal!  One of the weird things about driving here is the borders.  Because it’s the EU, the basically don’t exist.  If fact if there wasn’t a sign that said welcome to Portugal (in Portuguese of course) you would never know when you crossed the border.  So the tolls here are a little different than what I’m used to.  They have some open road electronic tolling, but the do the cash tolls a little differently. 

So when you enter the toll way, you grab a ticket and then when you leave the toll way, you stick the ticket in the machine and it charges you for distance.  This is a cool system and it makes things go pretty quick, but the only problem was that I totally didn’t understand this right away.  So when we got to the first booth, I was following another car and he was obviously Portuguese because he went through the electronic one. I followed him through the electronic one, but I didn’t know that I needed the ticket from the cash booth.

So then fast forward 200 km (look at me so European with my measurements).  I went to leave the highway and I went through the cash booth and the lady was like “oh you don’t have a ticket? So that’s a 50 Euro fine on top of the tolls”.  So that was bogus. 

At the end of it all we finally made it to Porto at about 12:00 AM.  We were kinda worried about finding parking, but there were plenty of signs and it was relatively easy.  The worst part was that some of the streets in Porto were SUPER small! I got stuck in one of them because I tried to make a left turn, from one of those super skinny streets onto another one.  It probably would have been fine, but people were parked on the sides of both of the streets so I had inches on either side.  To make it even better, there was tons of people walking around, because 12:00 means that people are heading out to go to the clubs.  I ended up having to back out of the whole street, but we made it with not a scratch on the BMW. 
The next day I woke up at about 8:30 and me and Matt went out to explore a little bit.  We decided to check out some of the places that looked interesting on the map, but also just to get out and see the city.



The first stop was a market.  We were thinking about maybe buying something to eat for breakfast. It was actually nothing like I imagined.  


I was thinking that it was going to be a pretty touristy, but it was actually kinda run down and pretty normal food items. 


There was nothing there that I really wanted, but I felt like I should buy something and so I bought some bread from a nice lady.

The next stop was the Crystal Palace.  This was a little hard to get to and again looked a lot cooler on the map.  


It wasn’t even a palace, it was just a small high school sized basketball stadium that had a lot of sun lights in it. 


When we walked inside, there was a book fair going on.


After the palace, we didn’t have too much time before we were gunna meet up with the other two girls we were traveling with to go on a walking tour.  So we decided to just make our way down through the gardens and walk along the river. 







On the way, we walked down some really small and winding streets.





We eventually made it down to the river side and we even saw a helicopter take off! Maybe I would have been inside if I had saved a few more pennies before coming here.


Continuing down the road we came upon this part where the road turned into a bridge.  It looked like the road was peeled off the side of the river.  It wasn’t really a bridge over anything and it didn’t really seem necessary, but it was cool nonetheless.  At one moment we were walking on solid ground and then suddenly we were walking on a grate over the water.










Eventually we made our way to the free walking tour (which FYI are never free.  You have to give them a “suggested tip at the end”).  The tour guide was fun and generally insightful.

On this tour I don’t think that there was very much that she had to say, and so most of it was just taking us around and showing us the big attractions and different places to get good views of the city.  I’ll just share some of the photos that I took along the way.

















After the tour she gave some suggestions on where to eat for lunch and so we decided to stop by there (actually basically all of the people on the tour decided to go). 

Since there was so many people it took a little while than it should have, but it was worth the wait! The food was awesome! I forgot what this was called, but it is like a sandwich with tons of different meats on it like beef, chorizo, bacon, and ham, then they melted cheese on top of it and poured some kind of gravy or béchamel over it.

It was already getting dark when we finished eating, but we went across to the other side of the river to get a better view of the main city of Porto.







After that it was basically dark. We wandered back to our hostel and did some souvenir shopping along the way.

We didn’t much more time awake because we had to get up early.  The garage where we parked our car was open 24H except for Sunday.  Its open until 7:00 AM.  So if we wanted to leave, we had to be there before then. 

All in all, it was a great day! It was pretty packed, but you need to do that if you only have one day in a city.  I really would have liked to spend at least one more day to be able to go inside of some of the buildings and museums that we saw. 
The city was nice and clean and there wasn’t really anyone there.  Both tourists and inhabitants.  In some of the pictures , you can see that there are some buildings along the river that are just completely gutted.  It’s just concrete pillars. Those lots should be full, its prime real estate along the river!

Portuguese is actually pretty mutually intelligible with Spanish.  It sounds like a French guy is trying to pronounce Spanish words.  So it’s a little less harsh and they have more “sh” sounds. 

But when we were talking with the attendant at the parking lot, we were able to understand each other enough.  He was able to tell me that even though the parking lot is usually by hour, some attendants will give you a deal if you are parking for longer than a day.  So it was a pretty complex idea, but with Portuguese and some hand motions, I was able to understand.  
So the next day, we woke up at the crack of dawn and went off on our journey back home. 



Oh yah, here is a picture of the car while we were filling it up!


We didn´t go straight back because that would be too boring! So we went up the coast towards the Northwest providence called Galicia.  Here there is the Cathedral de Compostela.  This Cathedral is the end of “El Camino de Santiago”. This is a very famous Catholic pilgrimage with paths from all over Europe. This is traditionally walked and takes months to complete and so sometimes people will only do part of it. 

Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela

There wasn´t much else there that we wanted to see, so we left pretty quickly.

I really wanted to pass through “Los Picos de Europa” (the Peaks of Europe), but we didn’t think that we would be able to make it back to Bilbao with enough time.  So instead, my friend Matt suggested that we go to “La playa de las Catedrales” (The Beach of Cathedrals). 

The beach was super close to the highway and it only took us about 15 minutes to get there and the beach was only a 5 min walk from the parking lot. 



Our visit was timed really well! It was an accident, but we showed up during low tide so we were able to pass through all the caves and arches and take some amazing pictures!





Even though we didn't go through the peaks, we did pass by them!


After this, we left for our final destination; Bilbao!  We arrived in Bilbao at about 7:00 and I went back home to take a fantastic and well deserved sleep. 

And look! They put up Christmas lights while we were gone! 

So the next week we have a really long break from school and I will be going to Istanbul and Greece. I won't be getting back until Wednesday, so I'll probably post the blog on the weekend!
